title: Org Types: Production, Sandbox, Scratch Org, Developer Edition, and Trailhead Playground
objectives: Name the main Salesforce org types and what each is for.
Choose the correct environment for learning, development, testing, or live business work.
Explain why production data must not be experimented on casually.
Distinguish long-lived sandboxes from disposable scratch orgs.
diagnostic_question: Your team has a live customer org, a full-copy sandbox, a scratch org from CI, and a Trailhead Playground. A new hire wants to 'practice deleting accounts.' Which org(s) are safe and why?
definition: A Salesforce org is a tenant environment. Production is the live org. Salesforce Help describes sandboxes as copies of your org in separate environments for development, testing, and training, without compromising production ([When to Use a Sandbox](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_sandboxes_intro.htm)). Scratch orgs are source-driven, fully configurable, disposable development environments created in relation to a Dev Hub; lifespan is 1 to 30 days and an expired scratch org cannot be restored ([Scratch Orgs](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_scratch_orgs.htm)). A Developer Edition org is a free org to try features and does not expire if you log in at least once every six months; you can also create Trailhead Playgrounds for hands-on challenges ([Developer Edition and Trailhead Playgrounds](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005298906)).
why_it_matters: Wrong-environment work causes data loss, compliance incidents, and confused debugging. Environment literacy is the first gate before configuration, coding, or integrations.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a teaching hospital. Production is the live operating room with real patients. A sandbox is a simulation suite copied from that hospital so you can practice without touching live cases. A scratch org is a pop-up drill tent you pitch for a few days and cannot restore after it comes down. Developer Edition and a Trailhead Playground are teaching wards: real Salesforce tools, not your company's production.
deeper_explanation: Production is the live org. Salesforce Help describes sandboxes as copies of your org in separate environments for development, testing, and training, without compromising production data and applications ([When to Use a Sandbox](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_sandboxes_intro.htm)).

Scratch orgs are source-driven, fully configurable, disposable environments for development and automated testing; they are created in relation to a Dev Hub, can be set to last 1–30 days, and cannot be restored after expiry ([Scratch Orgs](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_scratch_orgs.htm)).

Developer Edition is a free org to try features and does not expire if you log in at least once every six months. You can also create Trailhead Playgrounds for hands-on challenges ([How to Sign Up for Trailhead with a Developer Edition](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005298906)).

Learning orgs are not production: a Trailhead Playground is for challenges and practice. Feature-specific badges may require a different org type—Needs verification on the current challenge page. Sandbox entitlements remain edition-specific.

mental_model.analogy: A teaching hospital campus: the live operating room is production; simulation suites copied from that hospital are sandboxes; a pop-up drill tent is a scratch org; teaching wards are Developer Edition and Trailhead Playground orgs.
useful_mapping: simulation suite copied from the hospital → sandbox
pop-up drill tent with a scheduled teardown → scratch org
teaching ward → Developer Edition or Trailhead Playground
hospital administration that issues tents → Dev Hub
where_it_breaks: Simulation suites can still hold copied patient data—sandbox copies of production may include sensitive records.
A teaching ward is not a disaster-recovery site for the live operating room.
Scratch org expiration is 1–30 days and unrestorable; a tent analogy does not encode Dev Hub allocation limits.
Sandbox type, storage, and refresh entitlements vary by edition—Needs verification in the target production org.

teach_back_prompt: Explain production, sandbox, scratch org, Developer Edition, and Trailhead Playground using only the teaching-hospital analogy, then name one place the analogy breaks.

terminology.plain: The live Salesforce environment for real business.
terminology.precise: Customer tenant used for day-to-day operations with production data and integrations.
terminology.example: Company prod org where sales closes deals.
terminology.non_example: Trailhead Playground used for a badge.

terminology.plain: A non-production copy or template org for testing.
terminology.precise: Salesforce environment separated from production for build, test, or training.
terminology.example: Full sandbox configured with the required production-data copy for UAT.
terminology.boundary: Sandbox type limits vary by license.

terminology.plain: Sandbox with a large copy of production data and metadata.
terminology.precise: Sandbox tier intended to approximate production for integration and volume testing.
terminology.example: UAT cycle before a major release.
terminology.non_example: Developer sandbox with no production data.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Partial copy sandbox: targeted subset of production data.
terminology.boundary: Storage and refresh intervals are licensed.

terminology.plain: Short-lived dev org spun up from Dev Hub.
terminology.precise: Configurable Salesforce org created via Salesforce CLI for development, with expiration.
terminology.example: Feature branch CI creates scratch org for Apex tests.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Sandbox: isolated production copy for testing.
terminology.boundary: Requires Dev Hub and source-driven workflow.

terminology.plain: Free Salesforce org for learning and prototyping.
terminology.precise: No-cost org with limits, suitable for exploration—not implied production substitute.
terminology.example: Personal DE org for Flow experiments.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Trailhead Playground: tied to Trailhead modules.
terminology.boundary: Licensing and limits differ from paid prod.

terminology.plain: Learning org linked to Trailhead hands-on challenges.
terminology.precise: Developer Edition org configured for Trailhead hands-on challenges, with Trailhead-specific data and a pre-installed challenge-testing package; it has limits and never expires while you keep using it.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Developer Edition: free org for testing features and implementations; a Playground is a DE org with Trailhead-specific setup.
terminology.boundary: Use it for learning and safe experimentation away from production; limits apply, and some feature-specific badges require another org type.

terminology.plain: Org that can create scratch orgs.
terminology.precise: Enabled production or DE org acting as scratch org factory.
terminology.example: Team Dev Hub issuing scratch orgs in pipeline.

terminology.precise: Controlled path from dev/test orgs to production via deployment practices.
terminology.example: Metadata deployed sandbox → prod after sign-off.
terminology.non_example: Editing records directly in prod to 'test'.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Data refresh: copying data, not promoting config.
terminology.boundary: Full CI/CD is a later track.

when_to_use: When a teammate wants to practice deleting accounts and you must pick production versus a sandbox, scratch org, Developer Edition, or Trailhead Playground.
When CI needs a short-lived scratch org environment instead of a long-lived sandbox copy of production.
When UAT needs production-like data in a sandbox rather than a Trailhead Playground or empty scratch org.
When documenting which org types are allowed for learning, build, test, and live business work.
when_not_to_use: Do not use a Trailhead Playground or Developer Edition as a substitute for a licensed sandbox UAT of production.
Do not treat this org-types lesson as a full DevOps pipeline, change-set, or DevOps Center design.
Do not invent sandbox refresh intervals, storage caps, or edition entitlements; verify them in the target production org Help.
Do not use production as a scratch environment for experiments, even if the change looks small.

flashcards.front: What is a production org for?
flashcards.back: The live Salesforce environment for real business processes and customer data—not a practice lab.
An isolated copy of your org used for development, testing, and training without changing production.
A source-driven, disposable development org created from a Dev Hub, lasting 1–30 days and unrestorable after expiry.

flashcards.front: What is a Trailhead Playground used for?
flashcards.back: A free practice org for Trailhead hands-on challenges; Help also lets you connect a Developer Edition. Not a production substitute.

flashcards.front: What is a Developer Edition org?
flashcards.back: A free Salesforce org to try features. Help states it does not expire if you log in at least once every six months.

flashcards.front: Where should you practice deleting records?
flashcards.back: A non-production learning org or sandbox—never the production org with live customer data.

flashcards.front: Where do you run a prod-like integration test?
flashcards.back: A Full or Partial Copy sandbox that can copy production data; not a Trailhead Playground.

flashcards.front: Which org type fits a 7-day CI feature branch?
flashcards.back: A scratch org: default duration is 7 days, maximum 30, created from Dev Hub.

flashcards.front: Where do reps close live customer deals?
flashcards.back: Production, after the change has been tested in a sandbox or other approved non-production path.

flashcards.front: Where should a first-time Setup lab happen?
flashcards.back: A Trailhead Playground or Developer Edition—not production and not a Full sandbox full of customer PII.

flashcards.front: Can sandbox data still be sensitive?
flashcards.back: Yes. A sandbox copied from production can contain the same customer data; treat credentials and records accordingly.

flashcards.front: Is a Playground a production disaster-recovery site?
flashcards.back: No. A Trailhead Playground is a learning environment, not a substitute for production or a licensed UAT sandbox.

flashcards.front: Is a scratch org a permanent environment?
flashcards.back: No. After expiration it is deleted and cannot be restored; keep source in version control.

flashcards.front: Changes exist only in a sandbox. What next?
flashcards.back: Validate there, then deploy to production. Sandboxes do not auto-sync into the live org.

flashcards.front: A manager says to test in production. What do you say?
flashcards.back: Use an approved sandbox or other non-production path. Production is for live work after validation, not experiments.

flashcards.front: Playground versus Full sandbox for UAT—which and why?
flashcards.back: Full or Partial Copy sandbox when you need production-like data. A Trailhead Playground is for learning, not UAT fidelity.

interview_questions.question: Name the main Salesforce org types and what each is for.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Production is live business. Sandboxes are isolated copies for development, testing, and training. Scratch orgs are disposable Dev Hub environments lasting 1–30 days. Developer Edition and Trailhead Playgrounds are free learning orgs, not production.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I start with the workload. Live customer transactions belong in production after a tested deploy. Salesforce Help describes sandboxes as copies of the org in separate environments for development, testing, and training without compromising production. Scratch orgs are source-driven and disposable: you pick 1–30 days, default 7, and you cannot restore them after expiry. Developer Edition is a free org to try features; Help says it stays active if you log in at least every six months. A Trailhead Playground is a practice org for hands-on challenges. I never treat a Playground as UAT for production data.
interview_questions.example: UAT of a validation rule happens in a Full sandbox; the rule is deployed to production only after sign-off, never first tried on live deals.
tradeoffs: Data fidelity versus cost and refresh entitlements
Disposable scratch speed versus long-lived sandbox persistence
follow_ups: Which sandbox type would you pick for integration tests?
Where does source of truth live when a scratch org expires?
weak_answer_warnings: Treats Playground, sandbox, and production as interchangeable

interview_questions.question: Why must you not test destructive changes in production?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Production holds live processes and customer data. Salesforce provides sandboxes and other non-production org types so you can develop and test without compromising that live org.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Production is the system of record. A mass delete, a bad validation rule, or an untested Flow hits real users and integrations. Help’s sandbox guidance exists specifically so customization and testing stay isolated until you are ready to deploy. Scratch orgs and Developer Edition or Trailhead Playgrounds absorb learning risk, but they are not always production-like. I match fidelity to risk: Playground for a first Setup lab, sandbox for UAT, production only after promotion.
interview_questions.example: A new hire who deletes 200 Accounts 'to practice' in production caused a restore incident that a Developer sandbox would have contained.
tradeoffs: Perceived speed of testing in production versus customer and audit risk
follow_ups: How do you handle copied PII in a Full sandbox?
weak_answer_warnings: Says cloud computing means it is safe to experiment anywhere

interview_questions.question: The team has no sandboxes licensed. What do you recommend instead of testing in production?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I do not default to production experiments. I check whether a Developer Edition, scratch org via Dev Hub, or a Trailhead Playground can cover learning, and I escalate sandbox entitlements for UAT.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: First I name the risk: no sandbox does not make production a lab. Help documents Developer Edition as a free org to try features, and scratch orgs if a supported Dev Hub edition is available. A Trailhead Playground is fine for Setup practice. None of those automatically copies production data, so they are weak for realistic UAT. I document that gap, pursue the sandbox types the production edition actually includes—Needs verification—and refuse 'just be careful in prod.'
interview_questions.example: A small org on a lower edition uses Developer Edition for Flow trials and still waits for a licensed sandbox before UAT against production-like data.
tradeoffs: License cost versus the risk of untested production changes
follow_ups: Is Dev Hub available in this edition?
What data fidelity does UAT actually require?

interview_questions.question: A scratch org used for Friday's demo is gone on Monday. What happened and what do you do?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Scratch orgs expire after 1–30 days and cannot be restored. Recreate from source control and the scratch-org definition; do not expect Salesforce Support to undelete the org.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: The Salesforce DX Developer Guide states scratch orgs are temporary, deleted after expiration, with a maximum 30-day lifespan and a default of 7 days, and you cannot restore them. Persistent work belongs in git, not in the org. I check the duration that was set at creation, recreate from the project, and explain to stakeholders that a demo tenant is not a UAT sandbox. If they needed a longer-lived environment, a sandbox or Developer Edition would have been the better org type.
interview_questions.example: A 7-day default scratch org created Monday vanished the next Monday; the Apex classes were safe because they had been pushed to the repo.
tradeoffs: Disposable speed versus the need for a persistent demo org
follow_ups: Is Dev Hub enabled, and in which org?
What duration was set in the scratch-org definition?
weak_answer_warnings: Blames Salesforce data loss without mentioning the expiration policy

interview_questions.question: Users see different features in a sandbox than in production. How do you investigate?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I compare licenses, deployed metadata, and whether the sandbox is on a release preview. I do not assume a sandbox is a perfect twin of production without checking.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Help says sandbox behavior is similar to production but differences affect configuration and testing. I check login (correct sandbox versus production), last refresh, which metadata was deployed, and feature licenses. Preview sandboxes can be on the next seasonal release while production is not. A Trailhead Playground will almost never match production configuration. I gather evidence before claiming 'Salesforce is broken.'
interview_questions.example: A Flow action appears in a preview sandbox on the next release but not yet in production, so UAT and prod disagree until the production upgrade.
tradeoffs: Preview testing value versus temporary sandbox/production drift
follow_ups: When was the sandbox last refreshed?
Is this sandbox on a preview instance?
weak_answer_warnings: Assumes sandboxes automatically stay identical to production

interview_questions.question: An admin cannot find Sandboxes in Setup. What do you check before escalating?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Confirm they are in the production org, not a Trailhead Playground, and that they have permission to view sandboxes. Edition and licenses decide whether sandboxes exist at all.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Help documents sandbox creation from Setup in supported editions, with permissions such as View Setup and Configuration to view and Manage Sandboxes or Manage Dev Sandboxes to create. A Trailhead Playground or many Developer Edition orgs will not show a customer’s sandbox list. I verify the login URL, org Id, and user permissions, then check edition entitlements—Needs verification for that org—rather than telling them sandboxes do not exist as a product.
interview_questions.example: A new admin logged into a Trailhead Playground, searched for Sandboxes, and found nothing; production with Manage Sandboxes showed the list.
tradeoffs: Self-serve Setup versus opening a license ticket
follow_ups: Which org Id and login did they use?
Do they have Manage Sandboxes or only View Setup?
weak_answer_warnings: Claims sandboxes do not exist on the platform

interview_questions.question: Design an environment map for a 20-person Salesforce team.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I document production, at least one build sandbox, a UAT sandbox, scratch orgs for CI, and a separate Trailhead Playground or Developer Edition for learning—with a written promotion path.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Owners, allowed actions, and refresh cadence go on the map. Learning stays in Playground or Developer Edition so people do not practice on production data. Feature branches use scratch orgs from Dev Hub with source in git. UAT uses a sandbox that can hold the required production-like data. Production receives only deployed, signed-off metadata. Exact sandbox tiers and counts are edition-dependent, so I mark entitlements as Needs verification instead of inventing a Full-sandbox count.
interview_questions.example: A 20-person implementation uses Developer sandboxes for build, a Partial Copy for UAT, scratch orgs in CI, and forbids Trailhead Playgrounds for customer-data tests.
tradeoffs: License cost versus coverage of learning, build, UAT, and production
weak_answer_warnings: Proposes a single production org for all work

interview_questions.question: Explain a sandbox refresh to an executive in thirty seconds without jargon.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: A sandbox refresh updates the practice copy from production so testers see realistic configuration and, depending on type, data—without changing the live org the business uses.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Executives care about risk and realism. A sandbox is an isolated copy used for development, testing, and training. Refreshing it brings that copy up to date from production; it does not push sandbox experiments into production. Copied data can still be sensitive, so access and masking are part of the conversation. I do not quote a refresh interval unless I have verified that sandbox type’s entitlement for this edition.
interview_questions.example: Before a quarterly UAT, the team refreshes the Full sandbox so testers are not signing off on last year's metadata while production has moved on.
tradeoffs: Realistic testing versus storage, refresh windows, and copied PII
follow_ups: Do you mask PII in the sandbox?
Which sandbox type are we refreshing?
weak_answer_warnings: Gives only a technical deep dive or invents a universal refresh number
